blocks.text: A continuous random variable can take any value along an unbroken range, a person exact height, the time until a server crashes, or a pixel intensity produced by a generative model, rather than one value from a countable list. This lesson covers the probability density function that describes such variables, and the crucial fact that a density value is not itself a probability, only the area it traces out over a range is.

blocks.alt: A continuous random variable described by a density whose area gives probability
blocks.caption: From a continuous random variable to a density whose area equals probability

blocks.text: 1. What a Continuous Random Variable Is

A continuous random variable is one whose possible values fill an unbroken range with no gaps, rather than the countable list of separate values a discrete random variable takes, covered in the discrete random variables lesson elsewhere in this module. Height, weight, temperature, and time are the classic everyday examples.

Between any two possible values of a continuous random variable, no matter how close together, infinitely many other values are also possible, which is exactly why continuous random variables cannot be described with a simple table of individual outcome probabilities the way discrete ones can.

code.content:
import numpy as np
height_sample = np.random.normal(loc=170, scale=8)   # a single simulated continuous value
print(height_sample)

blocks.text: This uncountable, unbroken quality is exactly what separates a continuous random variable from the discrete random variables covered in the previous lesson, which can only ever take a countable list of separate values.
2. The Probability Density Function

The probability density function, almost always abbreviated PDF, describes how densely probability is packed at every point along a continuous range. Formally it is written f(x), and unlike the PMF from the discrete random variables lesson, f(x) is not itself a probability, a point covered in complete detail in section 3 below.

A PDF can be visualized as a curve drawn above the number line, taller sections of the curve mark ranges where values are more likely to occur, and shorter sections mark ranges that are comparatively rare.

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: A PDF that peaks sharply around 70 and tapers off toward 60 and 80 describes a random variable, like a test score, that is far more likely to land near 70 than near either extreme, even though every single exact value technically has 0 probability on its own.

blocks.text: 3. Why a Density Value Is Not a Probability

A PDF value f(x) can be greater than 1, which would be impossible for a genuine probability, since probabilities are always capped at 1 by the range rule from the probability rules lesson. This alone proves f(x) cannot be a probability in the same sense a PMF value is.

The probability of a continuous random variable landing on any single exact point is actually zero, since there are infinitely many possible points to divide 1 unit of total probability across. What a PDF actually gives a genuine probability for is the area underneath the curve over a range, not the height of the curve at a single point.

code.content:
from scipy import stats
normal_dist = stats.norm(loc=170, scale=8)
p_between_165_and_175 = normal_dist.cdf(175) - normal_dist.cdf(165)
print(p_between_165_and_175)   # a genuine probability, an area
print(normal_dist.pdf(170))     # a density value, not itself a probability, can exceed 1

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: A PDF value of f(170) equal to 0.05 does not mean there is a 5 percent chance of a height of exactly 170, it means the density near 170 is 0.05, and only integrating that density over a small range around 170, say 169 to 171, produces an actual probability number.

blocks.text: This is one of the most common early points of confusion in probability, a beginner naturally expects any probability-related function to stay between 0 and 1, but a density is a rate, not a probability itself, and rates can exceed 1 without breaking any rule.
4. Area Under the Curve Equals Probability

For a continuous random variable X, the probability that X falls between two values a and b is the area under the PDF curve between those two points, computed formally with an integral, but usually looked up in practice through a cumulative distribution function rather than computed by hand.

blocks.alt: Shaded area under a bell curve between two points a and b
blocks.caption: The shaded region between a and b is the probability, not the curve height itself

blocks.text: Wider intervals generally capture more probability, and narrower intervals capture less, which is exactly the behavior a rate-based measure like density should produce once it is properly integrated over a range.
5. The Cumulative Distribution Function

The cumulative distribution function, or CDF, of a continuous random variable gives P(X is less than or equal to x), the total area under the PDF curve from negative infinity up to x. Any range probability can be found by subtracting two CDF values, exactly the calculation shown in section 3 above.

code.content:
from scipy import stats
normal_dist = stats.norm(loc=170, scale=8)
print(normal_dist.cdf(170))   # 0.5, half the area lies below the mean
print(normal_dist.cdf(186))   # roughly 0.977, most area lies below two standard deviations up

blocks.text: The CDF always starts at 0 for very small values and rises to exactly 1 for very large values, since it accumulates probability across the entire range a random variable can take, mirroring the discrete random variable lesson cumulative distribution idea but built from an integral rather than a running sum.
6. Integrating a PDF Equals 1

The total area under a valid PDF curve, taken across every possible value the random variable could ever take, must equal exactly 1, the continuous counterpart to the sum-to-1 rule for a discrete PMF covered in the discrete random variables lesson.

In plain words, integrating means adding up infinitely many infinitesimally thin vertical strips under the curve, each contributing an almost-zero sliver of area, and the calculus machinery of an integral is simply the precise way of adding all those slivers together into one finite total.

code.content:
from scipy import integrate, stats
normal_dist = stats.norm(loc=170, scale=8)
total_area, _ = integrate.quad(normal_dist.pdf, -np.inf, np.inf)
print(round(total_area, 6))   # 1.0

blocks.text: This is the direct continuous counterpart of the sum-to-1 rule from the probability rules lesson, the same underlying requirement, every outcome accounted for exactly once, just expressed with an integral instead of a sum since there are infinitely many possible outcomes to account for.
7. The Normal Distribution

The normal distribution, also called the Gaussian distribution, is the single most common continuous distribution in statistics and machine learning, its PDF forms the familiar symmetric bell shaped curve, fully described by just two numbers, the mean, marking the center of the curve, and the standard deviation, controlling how spread out the curve is.

Many naturally occurring quantities, measurement error, human height within a population, and aggregated noise from many small independent sources, tend to follow something close to a normal distribution, a pattern formalized by the central limit theorem covered in its own lesson elsewhere in this curriculum.

code.content:
from scipy import stats
mean, std_dev = 170, 8
normal_dist = stats.norm(mean, std_dev)
print(normal_dist.pdf(170))   # peak density, at the mean
print(normal_dist.pdf(186))   # lower density, two standard deviations away

blocks.text: The normal distribution shape, a symmetric bell centered on its mean, is fully determined by just two numbers, the mean and the standard deviation, covered fully in its own lesson later in this module.
8. Plotting a PDF

Unlike the separated bars used to plot a discrete PMF, a continuous PDF is plotted as a single unbroken smooth curve, since values fill the entire range with no gaps between them, the smoothness of the curve itself visually communicates the continuous nature of the underlying random variable.

code.content:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
x = np.linspace(140, 200, 300)
plt.plot(x, stats.norm(170, 8).pdf(x))
plt.xlabel('Height')
plt.ylabel('Density')
plt.show()

blocks.text: Reading a PDF plot correctly means focusing on the shape and the relative area under different parts of the curve, not on the raw height of the curve at any single point, exactly the distinction covered in section 3.
9. The Uniform Continuous Distribution

The continuous uniform distribution assigns exactly the same density to every value across a fixed range, and zero density outside that range, the simplest possible continuous distribution to reason about and a useful contrast to the normal distribution bell shape covered above.

code.content:
from scipy import stats
uniform_dist = stats.uniform(loc=0, scale=10)   # uniform over the range 0 to 10
print(uniform_dist.pdf(5))    # 0.1, constant across the whole range
print(uniform_dist.cdf(5))    # 0.5, half the range lies below 5

blocks.text: This flat, constant density is exactly why the uniform distribution is the default choice whenever a random number generator is asked to produce a value with absolutely no preference for any particular part of its range.
10. Continuous Random Variables in AI Practice
10.1 Latent Variables and Generative Noise

A variational autoencoder represents its compressed internal representation of an input as a continuous latent variable, typically modeled with a normal distribution, sampling a new value from that latent distribution and decoding it is precisely how such a model generates new, previously unseen outputs.

Diffusion models work by repeatedly adding continuous Gaussian noise, sampled from a normal distribution, to training data and then learning to reverse that process step by step, generating new samples means running the learned reverse process starting from pure Gaussian noise.

items: Model weight initialization commonly draws each individual weight from a continuous normal or uniform distribution before any training begins.
Dropout style regularization techniques sometimes use a continuous random variable to decide how strongly to scale a given activation, rather than a purely on-off binary decision.
Confidence scores from certain probabilistic models are modeled as continuous random variables rather than a single fixed number, capturing the model own uncertainty about its own output.

blocks.text: 11. Standardizing a Normal Variable

Any normally distributed random variable can be converted into a standard normal variable, one with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, by subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation. This transformation, called a z-score, is covered fully in the standard deviation lesson later in this module, and it is what makes a single set of standard normal probability tables reusable for every possible normal distribution.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
x = 82
mean, std = 70, 8
z = (x - mean) / std
print(z)                          # 1.5
print(stats.norm.cdf(z))           # probability of landing at or below x

blocks.title: A concrete example
blocks.content: A test score of 82, drawn from a distribution with mean 70 and standard deviation 8, converts to a z-score of 1.5, meaning it sits 1.5 standard deviations above the mean, a comparison that works identically regardless of what the original units were, minutes, dollars, or points.

blocks.text: 12. Connection to Joint and Discrete Random Variables

Two or more continuous random variables can be described together with a joint probability density, extending the joint probability tables covered in the joint probability lesson elsewhere in this module from a discrete grid into a continuous surface, with marginalizing becoming an integral instead of a sum.

A single random variable can also mix discrete and continuous behavior, for instance the amount of rainfall on a given day is exactly zero with some real positive probability, but continuously distributed across all the positive rainfall amounts, a case that needs both PMF and PDF ideas from these two lessons combined.

Mixed models like this show up in practice whenever an outcome combines a yes-or-no decision with a measured quantity, such as whether a customer makes a purchase at all, discrete, and how much they spend if they do, continuous.
13. A Worked Example

A factory measures the time in minutes to assemble a component, and historical data shows this time follows a normal distribution with mean 12 minutes and standard deviation 2 minutes. Find the probability that a randomly chosen assembly takes between 10 and 14 minutes.

code.content:
from scipy import stats
assembly_time = stats.norm(loc=12, scale=2)
p_between = assembly_time.cdf(14) - assembly_time.cdf(10)
print(round(p_between, 4))   # roughly 0.6827

blocks.text: This 0.6827 figure is a specific case of a general pattern for the normal distribution, roughly 68 percent of all values fall within exactly one standard deviation of the mean in either direction, a useful rule of thumb worth remembering.

This assembly time example is a natural fit for the normal distribution since it reflects the sum of many small, independent sources of variation, worker speed, part tolerances, tool wear, exactly the kind of situation where a normal distribution tends to arise naturally.
14. Common Mistakes

items: Reading a PDF value directly as a probability, when only the area under a range of the curve is a genuine probability, exactly the mistake flagged in section 3.
Assuming a PDF value can never exceed 1, when in fact it can, especially for narrow distributions concentrated tightly around their mean.
Forgetting that the probability of a continuous random variable equaling one exact single point is always zero, and treating a specific point probability as though it were meaningfully nonzero.

Confusing standard deviation with variance when working with the normal distribution, standard deviation is the square root of variance, and scipy normal distribution functions expect standard deviation, not variance, as their scale argument.
Applying discrete-random-variable habits, like summing a finite list of outcomes, directly to a continuous problem that actually requires integrating or a CDF lookup instead.

blocks.text: A related trap worth naming directly: forgetting that the total area under any valid PDF must equal exactly 1, a function that looks like a reasonable density curve but integrates to something other than 1 is not a valid PDF at all.
15. Practice: Working with a Normal Distribution

A machine learning model latent variable is modeled as a normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, the standard normal distribution. Compute the probability that a sampled latent value falls between negative 1 and positive 1, and separately confirm the PDF value at 0 is greater than 1 over 2, illustrating that a density value alone is not a probability.

code.content:
from scipy import stats
standard_normal = stats.norm(0, 1)
p_between_neg1_and_1 = standard_normal.cdf(1) - standard_normal.cdf(-1)
print(round(p_between_neg1_and_1, 4))   # roughly 0.6827
print(standard_normal.pdf(0))            # roughly 0.3989, a density, well below 1 in this case

blocks.text: Try repeating the computation with a much smaller standard deviation, like 0.1, and notice the PDF peak value at 0 grows well past 1, direct evidence a density value is not bounded the way a genuine probability always is.

Notice how a smaller standard deviation concentrates more probability tightly around the mean, narrowing the range needed to capture the same 68 percent, a direct, hands on illustration of what standard deviation measures, covered fully in its own lesson ahead.
Key Takeaway

Standardizing a normal variable to a z-score, as covered in section 11, is the practical bridge that lets a single standard normal table or function answer probability questions for any normal distribution, regardless of its original mean or spread.

A continuous random variable is described by a probability density function rather than a probability mass function, and only the area under that density over a range gives a genuine probability, never the height of the curve at a single point. The normal distribution is the most common continuous distribution encountered in practice, and integrating any valid PDF across its entire range must always equal exactly 1.

Continuous latent variables and Gaussian noise sit at the heart of modern generative AI, from variational autoencoders to diffusion models, and the density-versus-probability distinction covered in this lesson is exactly the idea to keep straight when those models are covered in later, more advanced lessons.

The next lessons in this module, expectation, variance, and standard deviation, define precisely how to summarize a continuous or discrete random variable using just a few numbers, building directly on the density and area concepts introduced here.
